articles.title: East Yorkshire woman says endometriosis forced her to leave job
articles.summary: A charity says women should not have to choose between work and health because of endometriosis.
articles.body:
After years of suffering the pain of endometriosis, 21-year-old Charlotte Samphire was forced to leave her job because the symptoms were too severe to manage.

Now, the beauty therapist from East Yorkshire, along with Hull charity Hey Endo!, is hoping improvements will soon be made after a government report found the condition is having a significant impact on women's finances and careers.

"People need to know that women shouldn't have to choose between their careers and their health," she said.

Samphire, who has stage 4 endometriosis and has suffered years of debilitating pain since she was just 10 years old, said although her boss was understanding, she knows not everyone would be so lucky.

Endometriosis is a chronic condition in which cells that are similar to the lining of the womb grow in other parts of the body.

It can take an average of nine years to get a diagnosis from the onset of symptoms and it affects 1.5 million people in the UK.

The All-Party Parliamentary Group on Endometriosis recently published a report on the condition in the workplace, commissioned and funded by Endometriosis UK.

Kirsteen Sullivan MP, who is chairwoman of that group and also has endometriosis, said she wanted the government to introduce a national framework for women in the workplace.

"That framework should build on existing standards and the menopause action plans that were already introduced earlier this year," she said.

"I think that will provide support and guidance for employers so that they can better understand the support they should be providing to their employees, but also allow women living with the condition to better understand the kind of support they should receive."

She said the government should also review guidance around the Equality Act to ensure it better reflects fluctuating and chronic conditions.

Samphire said: "I worked in a salon and I loved working there, but I struggled to manage my endometriosis and I had to tell my employer that I couldn't fulfil my roles.

"Endometriosis changes women's lives every day, whether that's just being diagnosed or whether you've quit your job because you can't do it anymore, or whether it's taken over your mental health. It will do that to you.

"I believe the government should make it mandatory for employers to be educated on all conditions, whether they're visible or invisible, and the steps and support that they can take to help their employees.

"This could help so many women change their career paths, even change their lives."

Hey Endo! was co-founded by Helen Wilkinson, 34, and Ashleigh Hirst, 35. It became a registered charity in 2024 and now has more than 3,500 service users.

Last year, the charity launched a workplace Best Practice Charter in collaboration with the Hull and District Trades Union and Hull West and Haltemprice MP Emma Hardy.

Wilkinson said: "I went through 17 jobs in 14 years and a lot of it was due to sickness absence.

"I would either lose the job because I had too much time off or I would leave the job before they could sack me because I had too much time off."

She said some employers have been "absolutely brilliant" and tried to understand but in other workplaces the understanding simply wasn't there.

"Almost everybody who comes into our service from the beginning, within six months they're in a much better place with themselves," she said.

"They're a lot stronger and able to go out and advocate for themselves and they know their rights.

"For a lot of them, it's often a case of basic information that they weren't aware of, just directing them to things like the Equality Act and having a word with their occupational health team at work."

Hirst says her endometriosis symptoms started to appear around the age of 11. She describes her diagnosis, at the age of 25, as a "big wake-up call".

"I was just recently married but all of these symptoms came in a great big wave and just knocked me off my feet," she said.

"Being on the floor in pain and vomiting through the pain, I thought that was normal and I thought everyone went through it and I just kept it behind closed doors, but actually it's not normal."

Hirst says Hey Endo! would like the government to speak to local charities like theirs if a new national framework on endometriosis is developed.

"We have said for many years that there are so many women in the workplace who don't feel supported, who maybe feel like they have to change jobs and careers.

"It absolutely has to happen sooner rather than later."

A government spokesperson said: "For millions of women, endometriosis has a serious impact on their wellbeing, relationships and participation in the workforce.

"The government's Renewed Women's Health Strategy identifies endometriosis as a priority condition and states our commitment to improve the treatment and ongoing care for every woman affected."

articles.title: Shropshire and Worcestershire soft play centres face challenges
articles.summary: Jessica Harvey from Whitchurch said there were some days in the summer that no-one visited her centre.
articles.body:
The owner of a soft play area in north Shropshire said it is in danger of closure as the hot summer has meant centres like hers have struggled to get people through the doors.

Jessica Harvey has run Funzone in Whitchurch for over a year, and said the industry is seasonal, with there being occasions when she was the only one at the centre all day.

"Over the summer, there has definitely been [times] where we probably had 10 to 15 people in all week, which just isn't sustainable", she said.

Funzone, which has existed as a soft play centre in Whitchurch for 17 years, was sold two years ago. But the company that bought it went into liquidation, meaning Harvey was able to buy the firm in October 2025.

She said her first hot summer has been extremely challenging.

"It has been a bit demoralising. We have tried so hard to bring things back, and obviously when you are investing heavily, but not only just investing, a lot of our time has gone into it too.

"I'm talking getting up at six o'clock in the morning, being there for four hours before opening, and then not leaving the place until 12 at night because you're painting or building."

Harvey added that she was able to make the money up by building a soft play trailer built for events, but said that with the weather getting colder, she would need people to start coming again.

"Eventually, if no one uses it and there was no money coming in, it's not a viable business, is it?" she said.

"So, you know, it would have to go. It [is a] kind of use it or lose it type situation."

Connor Galbraith and his wife Nicole opened Wacky Playland in Kidderminster nearly two years ago, leaving their jobs as an IT specialist and a chemist.

The pair posted to their social media pages to share the reality of what the cost of running the centre.

"Three months of usage of electricity cost us £9,756.42; building insurance per year, is £6,410.47. That's just the building paid for the landlord's insurance, not including our public liability, [or] employee liability insurance as well," Galbraith added.

"We have a service charge as well, every three months, that is £5,837.33.

"Some customers do not realise the prices behind it, they just see it as, 'oh it's a business'."

He added their aircon and the 5% VAT relief helped them keep their business going through the summer.

However, Galbraith said the business could still pay the bills but it was "really tight."

"If costs keep going higher and higher then it does kind of question where we can be because, I'm sure any business owner knows, that we have a lease as a 10-year lease and as goes up incrementally." Galbraith said.

"If, as years go by, our rent is going to go higher and if, in this world how it's looking things are going to get more expensive, then it kind of makes you scared, like where is it going to be."

Last month, the owners of The Kidz Barn, also in Kidderminster, announced their soft play centre would be closing its doors in January 2026, and would be put up for sale.

In a social media post, the centre said it "was not a decision that was made lightly."

"We weathered some incredibly difficult times. During COVID, there were moments when we genuinely didn't know if we would ever reopen our doors.

"Somehow, we got through those hardest months, and being able to welcome you all back was something we will never forget."

articles.title: How to get Tandridge District Council's £250 cost of living help
articles.summary: Applications for household grants of up to £250 are opening to some Surrey residents.
articles.body:
Applications for household grants of up to £250 are due to open for residents in part of Surrey.

Tandridge District Council is funding the scheme, which last ran in January, to support residents with the cost of living .

Applicants must live in the Tandridge district, be over 16 years old and be "experiencing financial hardship", the council says.

They must also prove they are struggling to pay for essential items for themselves or their dependants by submitting full bank statements for August, September and October.

Other evidence such as arrears letters and energy bills can be uploaded too.

Grants are available to households even if they receive support from elsewhere, such as Surrey County Council funds .

Tandridge District Council said it aimed to provide support to those who needed help the most.

Successful applicants will receive a one-off payment, with the soonest payment date at the end of November.

Households without children can apply for £150, while those with under 18s can apply for £250.

The scheme is worth a total of £150,000 and applications will be processed on a first come, first served basis, the council said.

Other authorities in the county offer their own cost of living support.

Residents can apply online or by phone from 10:00 GMT on 9 November.

People who apply by phone will have to take their bank statements to the council's offices in Oxted.

Applications close on 31 December at the latest.

articles.title: Upton Magna parents oppose plans for battery site near school
articles.summary: Plans for the site put it less than a kilometre from St Lucia's CofE Primary School and Nursery
articles.body:
A group of parents whose children attend a rural primary school have said they are concerned by proposals to build a battery storage plant nearby.

These sites, also known as battery energy storage systems (BESS), hold energy generated from wind or solar and release it when needed, but there are concerns about fire safety due to the lithium used in the batteries.

Elgin Energy's plans for the site would put it less than one kilometre from St Lucia's Primary School and Nursery in Upton Magna, Shropshire.

The firm has said it has "taken on board guidance from Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service and the National Fire Chiefs Council" when designing the site.

Planning documents state that the school is 811 metres from a "potential fire source", although local residents have claimed 610 metres is a more accurate figure.

Kryssy Sochacki's daughter is a student at the primary school, and feels "terrified" by the prospect.

"My main focus has been around the safety of the school," she said.

"We fully recognise the importance of renewable energy," Sochacki added, but said "the pursuit of renewable energy shouldn't come at the expense of children's safety".

"This is just far too close to the school."

The excess electricity is stored in BESS, usually inside lithium-ion batteries, so when conditions are calm and overcast it can be sent back into the power grid.

Concerns around fire safety stems from the lithium within the batteries, which can cause an explosion when it overheats.

A fire at a battery storage unit in Nottinghamshire in May 2026 saw residents advised to keep doors and windows closed.

In planning documents, the school is noted to be one of the locations "at greatest risk" of being affected by smoke in the event of a fire.

The smoke plume assessment suggests that "winds from the southwest" could carry smoke towards the school "approximately 18% of the time during a fire event".

In its planning application, submitted by agents Berry's, Elgin Energy said it had consulted both Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service and the National Fire Chiefs Council".

It also said the plans for the 10-acre site had been drawn up with "safety as a priority".

It said that included measures including "fire detection in each container, over-temperature protection, ventilation systems, and aerosol fire extinguishing system".

Of the 87 public comments on Shropshire Council's planning portal, 85 are objections and just two are in support.

According to the National Fire Chiefs Council , "BESS fires are challenging to extinguish and can continue to burn from several hours to several days."

Its guidance adds that "smoke plumes from fires can also harm air quality" and that attempting to extinguish a BESS fire using water could "result in large volumes of contaminated fire-water runoff which can have a long-term impact on the environment".

As such, the NFCC said the "prevailing view" was to adopt a "controlled burn to minimise runoff."

Stef Thomas has two children at the primary school, and said the close proximity of the battery site was her main concern.

"If there was a fire, the wind blows in [the direction of the school] more often than not," she said.

"It's frightening, honestly, it's a massive worry.

"Why would we want any sort of chance, any sort of risk to our children, even with like a 1% chance?"

Laura Potts, another parent, said: "It's really concerning, and it's frightening."

She added that she wanted to see more communication "on what would happen in an emergency".

"The safety of the children is of the utmost importance," Potts said.

"I think the safety of our children in the schools should be considered more important than even the education itself."

The area is represented on Shropshire Council by Reform UK's Brendan Mallon, who said he had "many concerns" about the BESS plans.

Mallon said he feared that a fire at the site could "shut down" the adjacent A5, which in turn could, he said, affect the ability of the emergency services to respond.

He added that he believed battery storage plants should instead be built on "remote sites, preferably industrial sites".

Mallon said that should the BESS be approved, he would feel "extremely let down," adding that the potential impact on the school "should have been applied at the start and rejected".

A spokesperson for Shropshire Council said that "all planning applications are considered on their merits," with comments raised as part of the consultation taken into account.

Elgin Energy, planning agent Berry's, and St Lucia's CofE Primary School and Nursery have all been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Could a law change 'complete' Daniel O'Connell's legacy?
articles.summary: Legislation still exists that bars Roman Catholics from exercising the responsibility of presenting the monarch with a candidate to head the Church of England.
articles.body:
It's only taken 200 years but one of Ireland's most significant figures could finally have his legacy "completed".

Daniel O'Connell, a lawyer and politician, known as 'The Liberator', successfully campaigned for Catholics to have more rights in Parliament in the 1820s, but some restrictions on their roles still apply.

Streets in Dublin have been named after him, but there is little recognition of him in the halls of Westminster.

The Kerry-born man - who was described at the time as "the greatest popular leader the world has ever seen" by Liberal Party Prime Minister William Gladstone - is back on people's minds with new legislation that he would certainly have championed.

The Church Appointments (Repeal of Discriminatory Provision) Bill has been described as removing "the last remaining discriminations against Catholics and Jews" in Parliament.

It must be approved by the House of Commons and House of Lords before any change would come into practice. The bill is currently awaiting its second reading in the Lords.

O'Connell achieved Catholic Emancipation through the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829 after he was elected as the Member of Parliament for Clare, thus allowing him to take his seat in the House of Commons.

The act removed some of the restrictions on Catholics' participation in public life.

However some of those restrictions have been brought back into the public eye almost 200 years later with the United Kingdom having its first Catholic prime minister, Andy Burnham.

When appointing bishops and archbishops, the Church of England presents a candidate to the prime minister who then advises the monarch - as they are the head of the Church - on who to install in the role.

Although the involvement of the prime minister in this process has become more of a formality in recent years, legislation still exists that specifically bars Roman Catholics and Jews from exercising this responsibility.

He was born in County Kerry in 1775 when Catholics were under severe political restrictions and civil restrictions.

He was sent to France for school at a time of political upheaval that shaped his non-violent outlook on life.

When he achieved Catholic Emancipation it left him with "an incredible legacy", Prof Patrick Geoghegan from Trinity College Dublin told BBC News NI.

While not being a strict Catholic himself, O'Connell allowed Catholics to feel "like they were equal in their own country", according to the academic.

"It was all achieved through exclusively peaceful means, where other Irish revolutionaries and radicals and reformers had used violence and had failed," Geoghegan said.

"Daniel O'Connell showed the world that you were able to achieve massive change through mobilising the people, through using exclusively democratic means, through engaging with people, and by ensuring that the voice of a people could never be silenced.

"He brought an entire country behind him."

After entering the House of Commons in 1830, O'Connell ultimately failed in his attempt to dissolve the Act of Union - passed in 1800, it had abolished the Irish Parliament and united Ireland and Great Britain at Westminster.

Will O'Connell's legacy be fulfilled by the bill?

During a debate on the bill in the House of Commons last month, MP for Ealing Southall, Deirdre Costigan said "there is no statue or portrait to O'Connell in this House".

"Does the minister agree that today, 197 years on, the legacy of Daniel O'Connell, the Liberator, will finally be complete with full equality in elected office for both Catholics and Jews?"

Speaking to BBC News NI, Costigan said the bill "is the final instalment, really, of the long fight that Daniel O'Connell was involved in".

"So I think it's a nice thing to celebrate that."

She added that the 200th anniversary of the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829 is coming up "shortly" and "it has taken a while" to remove the last remaining restrictions.

Costigan said it was a "sad thing" that there was no statues or portraits of O'Connell in Parliament "because he had a huge impact".

"He was a big campaigner for the abolition of slavery and was very involved in lots of the debates of the day. He was a great orator," she said.

"I think there may be moves afoot now with some parliamentarians, myself included, to see if we can get that addressed, perhaps for the 200th anniversary."

Being an MP who is also from Ireland, Costigan said she feels the legacy of O'Connell.

"People often say to me 'my gosh, you're Irish and you're sitting in the British Parliament' and actually, that's a great thing about this country," she said.

"Obviously, I love Ireland, but I've lived here now longer than I lived in Ireland and it is a fantastic country, so welcoming from people across the world."

Cottigan added she is mindful of the long history of Irish MPs at Westminster and the influence they had.

"That does give you the kind of the bravery to be able to stand up in what is still... a very strong Irish accent.

"It's a legacy of people like Daniel O'Connell."

Geoghegan thinks O'Connell would be "amused" that, almost 200 years after "his greatest achievement", it's only now these "last remaining elements" could be removed.

"I think he would also be impressed with the scale of the change and the fact that you do have a Catholic as prime minister and it's not an object of controversy."

He added that while there may be no statues or portraits in Westminster, O'Connell "isn't forgotten".

O'Connell's message remains as relevant today as it was in the 19th Century, amid challenges such as political polarisation, declining trust in institutions and threats to human rights, he added.

"I think he is still very relevant, and I think in the years ahead, we will find him increasingly talked about, celebrated, and remembered."

articles.title: Why we disrupted Annalena Baerbock’s award speech
articles.summary: The former German foreign minister is no proponent of peace and justice. No award can wipe out her disastrous record.
articles.body:
When, in late August, the Dag Hammarskjold Foundation announced that former German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock was its 2026 medallist, we were stunned. The cognitive dissonance was striking, even if we had become used to this after years of unabashed hypocrisy within the world’s most powerful institutions.

According to the foundation’s homepage , the medal is given to a person who “contributes to a more just, peaceful and environmentally sustainable world through valuable achievements in politics or research”.

As this year’s medallist, Baerbock was invited to visit Uppsala University and deliver a lecture. Here was an event claiming to celebrate “ compassion, humanism and commitment to international solidarity ” while honouring the foreign minister of a government that approved 94 million euros ($102m) in arms exports to Israel in the span of three months in 2024.

The motivation provided for Baerbock’s selection as the 2026 Dag Hammarskjold medallist sounded like satire to us. She is described as a “strong proponent of a rules-based international order” even though her actions illustrate perfectly how she is the opposite of that.

As soon as Uppsala University started promoting the ceremony on campus, we decided to plan a protest. Baerbock needed to know that she was not welcome, that the university’s stance did not reflect the position of its students.

We entered the event split into groups and interrupted Baerbock’s seminar four times. She was increasingly frustrated with each interruption. She tried to respond to the argument of the first group with an incoherent ramble about an alleged misfired Palestinian rocket. But we were not arguing over a single rocket; we were criticising her unapologetic support for horrific violations of international law.

As foreign minister, Baerbock repeatedly expressed her strong support for the state of Israel as an occupying power, declaring that Israel’s security also is “ in the interest of the German state ”. As Germany’s foreign minister, she called it her responsibility to always defend Israel’s “security” – something she deemed “ non-negotiable for Germany ”.

She had no reservations about upholding Israeli claims that it had the right to target schools, hospitals and other civilian establishments because the alleged presence of resistance forces removed their protected status .

Baerbock has held these positions despite the International Court of Justice indicating provisional measures against Israel with the intention to encourage the international community to take action against the genocide in Gaza and despite the International Criminal Court issuing an arrest warrant for Israeli leaders on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Instead, Baerbock chose to fuel the fire.

For all of these efforts, she was “rewarded” with the position of president of the United Nations General Assembly. Even in that role – in the heart of the institution that is supposed to uphold international law – she refused to call what is happening in Gaza a genocide. This is despite multiple reports, including by UN experts, that this is exactly what the mass killing is.

That Uppsala University co-organised Baerbock’s lecture is not surprising. The university continues to refuse to implement even the most modest of measures against an occupying power that openly commits genocide .

In 2022, the university administration showed no hesitation in ending collaboration with Russian institutions after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Three years into the genocide in Gaza and the intensified ethnic cleansing of the occupied West Bank, it has taken no such action against Israeli institutions, despite repeated demands from students and faculty.

Yet we are grateful for this perfect opportunity to demonstrate why radical resistance is necessary. For many years, protests against the genocide in Palestine have obeyed the rules defined by those in power, without any effect. Palestinians have been killed while places of higher education refuse to take responsibility and diplomats utter nothing but hollow words.

If they will not listen to voices within their regulated framework, we see no choice but to disrupt their everyday efforts to hide their complicity.

We are criticised for our methods because they are “too much”. But for us, genocide is too much. Disagreeing politely and hearing out those who sell bombs to genocidal armies is what has brought us to this point of deadly inaction.

The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Poland mass shooting assailant dies in hospital, police say
articles.summary: Suspect shot by police and arrested minutes ‌after gunfire opened on people in central Krakow.
articles.body:
The gunman who killed six people and wounded more than a dozen in central Krakow last week has died in hospital, police say.

“We inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died this morning in the hospital,” police wrote in a post on X on Monday.

The 24-year-old Polish man was shot by police officers and arrested on Saturday minutes ‌after gunfire was opened on people at Krakow’s historic main square. The man opened fire from his car, police said.

The square is a major tourist destination in the country’s second-largest city, and several foreigners were among the dead and wounded.

Investigators also found the bodies of the suspect’s sister, mother and father at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a city 200km (125 miles) northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds.

Prosecutors on Sunday opened an investigation into an “act of terrorism”, and Poland’s interior minister said the suspect was fascinated by “far-right ideologies”.

The man carried out the attack in full military fatigues and wore “many different emblems” that investigators have “partially examined ⁠and interpreted”, a spokesperson for the Ministry of the Interior and Administration told Polish media.

Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, authorities said. A man from the United Kingdom and a woman from Austria were also among the dead.

The two police officers who stopped the gunman in actions authorities hailed as heroic were injured and remain in hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon.

Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the United Kingdom, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

Krakow attracts millions of tourists per year, and the city’s Main Market Square is a major tourist attraction often bustling with activity.

On Sunday, mourners laid candles and flowers near bullet holes at the square.

articles.title: Who are the seafarers caught in the US-Israeli war on Iran?
articles.summary: International Maritime Organization records at least 25 deaths since the conflict started on February 28.
articles.body:
Commercial vessels moving through the Strait of Hormuz and its surrounding waters have come under repeated attack since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran nine months ago.

The conflict has transformed one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors into a dangerous passage for crews transporting oil, gas and other goods.

On Sunday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three “rogue oil tankers travelling an unauthorised route” in the strait were subject to “explosions and severe fires”.

The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has recorded the deaths of at least 25 seafarers since the war started on February 28. Many of those killed have been citizens of India, one of the world’s largest suppliers of merchant sailors.

“It is unacceptable that throughout this conflict seafarers have been placed in harm’s way,” the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), a shipping trade association and advocacy group, told Al Jazeera.

“It is incumbent on all parties to take all necessary steps to safeguard the safety of seafarers who are simply going about their job and have found themselves, through no fault of their own, in a highly volatile situation,” an ICS spokesperson added.

The latest incidents have raised questions about the safety of civilian crews, their ability to refuse dangerous assignments and the protections available under international law.

What is happening to ships in the Strait of Hormuz?

The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial passage for international shipping, Before the war, roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passed through the waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Arabian Sea.

Iran essentially closed the strait after the US-Israeli attacks began, warning that ships trying to sail through the waterway without authorisation could be targeted. Meanwhile, Washington has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

Attacks on shipping have involved missiles, projectiles and naval mines that have damaged vessels, set them on fire or sunk them. According to the IMO, at least 129 incidents have been reported.

On Thursday, Iranian forces said five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents in the strait.

Separately, a Marshall Islands-flagged tanker named Velos Sapphire suffered an explosion north of Qatar, killing one crew member.

October was particularly dangerous for commercial shipping with at least 31 vessels hit.

Who are the seafarers being killed or injured?

The victims are largely civilian merchant sailors working on oil tankers, cargo ships and other commercial vessels.

Many come from countries far removed from the conflict, including India, whose nationals have suffered particularly heavy losses, with at least 16 killed.

In June, three Indian sailors were killed in US strikes on commercial vessels near Oman, prompting New Delhi to summon a senior American diplomat.

On Tuesday, Gandhar Nahim Ajij from Gujarat died after the cargo vessel MSV Al Jusufi was struck off Oman. Thirteen other Indian crew members were rescued.

In October, 12 crew members were injured when the Panamanian-flagged tanker On Peace was struck near Oman. Eleven of those injured were Indian nationals.

People from other countries have also been among the dead. In September, two Filipino crew members were killed when the Saudi tanker Sidr was hit by projectiles near the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian civilian maritime workers have also suffered casualties.

In May, the head of Iran’s merchant marine union said at least 44 Iranian seafarers had been killed and 29 injured since the start of the war.

What other challenges do seafarers face?

Beyond the threat of death or injury, the war has also taken a toll on sailors’ mental health, according to the ICS spokesperson.

“Shipowners are working hard to ensure that impacted seafarers have access to mental health support services as well as increased access to calls with family and friends,” the spokesperson added.

About 6,000 seafarers remained stranded near the Strait of Hormuz in October, the IMO said in late August.

In March, an arrangement was negotiated between maritime unions and shipping companies through the International Bargaining Forum, under which seafarers could refuse to enter designated danger zones and receive company-funded repatriation and compensation equivalent to two months of basic wages.

At the same time, the International Transport Workers’ Federation said the agreement also provides for increased wages and twice the standard compensation for seafarers who die or suffer a disability.

However, those protections do not necessarily cover every seafarer. And seafarers in the Gulf also face grave mental suffering, maritime charities warned in May, saying many faced loneliness, anxiety and distress.

“As we have throughout the conflict, we strongly urge all ships operating in the region to conduct thorough risk assessments and to maintain vigilance in line with the latest BMP [best management practices] maritime security guidelines,” the ICS spokesperson said.

What does international law say about protecting seafarers during the war?

Under Article 38 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, ships and aircraft “enjoy the right of transit passage” , a right that no country may suspend.

Article 17 also guarantees foreign vessels the “right of innocent passage” through another country’s territorial waters. Under Article 19, such passage is considered innocent provided it is not “prejudicial to the peace, good order or security of the coastal state”.

While the IMO in June sought arrangements to evacuate stranded sailors, efforts to establish safe passage have faced repeated obstacles as attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue unabated.

Academic Abdul Khalique says while international law undoubtedly does apply, “its enforcement is the weak link.”

“The law is clear on the obligations. The gap is political will and practical enforcement,” Khalique, head of the Liverpool John Moores University Maritime Centre, told Al Jazeera.

“For seafarers themselves, legal protections matter most when paired with operational avoidance.”

articles.title: Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina seeks passport in sign of Bangladesh return plan
articles.summary: Hasina, who has been living in India for two years, has promised to return to Bangladesh in December.
articles.body:
Bangladesh’s ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has requested a new passport and identity card to allow her to return from self-imposed exile in India.

The request is the clearest sign that Hasina, who has been living in India for two years, plans to make good on her promise that she would return to Bangladesh in December.

Hasina told the Reuters news agency that she intended to surrender before a court in Bangladesh, and her aides said on Monday the date would be announced once various formalities were completed.

Bangladesh’s war crimes court sentenced Hasina to death in absentia last November for ordering a deadly crackdown on student protests that swept the country in 2024 . As many as 1,400 people may have been killed in the violence, according to United Nations estimates.

Hasina’s letter to the Bangladeshi government, cited by Reuters, asked that her request be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of her Bangladeshi nationality.

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the foreign and law ministries were looking into the matter, including whether there was any legal basis for the applications and whether Hasina was legally entitled to apply for the documents, the Dhaka-based English-language New Age daily reported.

Last week, Junior Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said Bangladesh wants Hasina returned under an extradition treaty with India. New Delhi has declined to hand her over.

“We want Hasina to be handed over. She will be handed over. She is a terrorist. She is a fugitive. There is an active extradition treaty between Bangladesh and India,” he told reporters in Dhaka on Thursday.

Hasina is the daughter of Bangladesh’s founder and first president, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. She served as prime minister from 1996 to 2001, and again from 2009 to 2024.

Hasina’s potential return raises the prospect of renewed legal and political issues in the country.

She still enjoys support among parts of the population, and her return could affect the Bangladeshi government’s efforts to stabilise the country and its economy after two years of disruption.

Hasina was ousted by a popular, student-led mass protest movement that broke out after the Supreme Court restored a job quota system that had prioritised the descendants of the country’s liberation activists.

articles.title: Which countries and industries emit the most greenhouse gases?
articles.summary: The US has emitted the most CO2 in history; China is now the biggest emitter. Here’s who is driving global emissions.
articles.body:
World leaders and delegates are gathering in Antalya, Turkiye, for COP31 , the annual climate summit of the United Nations, which runs from November 9 to 20.

They meet as global emissions continue to climb. The world emitted 54.1 billion tonnes of greenhouse gases in 2025, 0.7 percent more than the year before and 68.5 percent more than in 1990, according to the latest figures from the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC) and the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Greenhouse gases, mainly carbon dioxide and methane, trap heat in the atmosphere, raising global temperatures and fuelling heatwaves, droughts, floods and other extreme weather conditions.

In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera breaks down which gases are warming the planet, which industries and countries emit the most, and how their emissions have changed over time.

Carbon dioxide (CO2) made up 73.8 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025. It is released mainly when fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas are burned, while deforestation removes trees that would otherwise absorb it.

Methane (CH4) accounted for 17.6 percent of emissions that year, followed by nitrous oxide (N2O) at 5.3 percent and fluorinated gases (F-gases) at 3.3 percent.

Global CO2 emissions have risen by 76.3 percent since 1990, according to the JRC.

How is a warming planet affecting the world?

As these gases build up in the atmosphere, they trap more heat. In 2025, the heat stored in the world’s oceans reached its highest level on record, and the rate of ocean warming has increased sharply over the past two decades, according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

Extreme weather has killed tens of thousands of people and forced millions from their homes in 2026, according to the WMO.

In Europe, heatwaves, droughts and wildfires between May and August caused more than 30,000 excess deaths, and 220,000 people were evacuated in France alone.

On August 26, a glacier collapse and the resulting flash flood in the Himalayas killed more than 1,500 people in Nepal along its border with China, while about 5,600 remain missing, according to the UN.

In June and July, Typhoon Bavi forced three million people to evacuate in China and killed 26 in the Philippines. Weeks later, severe Tropical Storm Maysak killed 171 people and caused more than $3bn in losses in China.

Earlier in the year, floods and windstorms across the western Mediterranean displaced more than 180,000 people in Morocco, while extreme cold and snow in North America killed 174 people.

The map below shows some of the most extreme weather events of 2026.

Where do the world’s emissions come from?

The world’s greenhouse gas emissions have more than doubled since 1970, rising from about 23 billion tonnes to 54.1 billion tonnes in 2025, according to the JRC.

The power industry, which generates electricity, is the largest source, producing nearly 30 percent of global emissions in 2025. Its emissions have roughly quadrupled since 1970, driven by soaring demand for electricity in fast-growing economies such as China and India.

Industry, including manufacturing and mining, is the second-largest source at 21 percent. This covers fuel burned in factories as well as gases released when producing cement, metals and chemicals. Industrial emissions climbed steeply in the 2000s as China’s manufacturing boomed.

Transport, including cars, shipping and aviation, is third at 16 percent.

Together, these three sectors produce about two-thirds of the world’s emissions. The rest comes from agriculture (12 percent), the extraction of coal, oil and gas (11 percent), buildings (6.6 percent) and waste (3.6 percent).

Global emissions have fallen only a handful of times since 1970, including in the early 1980s, after the 2008 financial crisis and during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Each time, they rebounded.

Who are the largest emitters of greenhouse gases?

In 2025, the three largest emitters produced almost half of the world’s greenhouse gases. China emitted almost 16 billion tonnes (29.5 percent), the United States 6.02 billion tonnes (11.1 percent) and India 4.51 billion tonnes (8.3 percent).

The 27 countries of the European Union together accounted for 5.8 percent, followed by Russia (4.8 percent), Indonesia (2.5 percent), Brazil (2.4 percent) and Iran (2.1 percent).

International shipping and aviation, which fall outside any single country’s total, together produced 2.6 percent of global emissions, more than most countries.

It was not always this way. The Industrial Revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries drove up emissions first in the West, particularly in the United Kingdom and the US, as they built factories and moved to mass manufacturing. Global emissions then rose sharply after World War II and have more than doubled since 1970.

China’s emissions surged in the early 2000s as its economy boomed, and it overtook the US as the world’s largest emitter in the mid-2000s.

But measured over time, the picture changes. Since the mid-18th century, the US has produced 23.5 percent of all CO2 emissions, compared with 15.4 percent from China, according to the Global Carbon Budget.

Which industries drive each country’s emissions?

In China, the power sector is the largest source, producing 42 percent of the country’s almost 16 billion tonnes of greenhouse gases. Industry accounts for 31 percent and fuel production for 9.5 percent.

In September 2025, Chinese President Xi Jinping, for the first time, pledged to cut the country’s greenhouse gas emissions by 7 to 10 percent from their peak by 2035.

In the US, transport is the largest source at 29 percent, mostly from cars and trucks. The power sector accounts for 26 percent and industry for 14 percent.

In India, which still relies heavily on coal for electricity, the power sector produces 35 percent of emissions, followed by industry at 24 percent and agriculture at 19 percent.

articles.title: Ava Marie Musci of Liverpool, New York, set up a lemonade stand at age 8 to fight childhood cancer; ten years later she has raised $22,000, enough to fund 450 hours of research, and been named one of the area’s best
articles.summary: Ava Marie Musci of Liverpool, New York, was eight years old when she decided to do something to help children fighting cancer.
articles.body: Ava Marie Musci of Liverpool, New York, was eight years old when she decided to do something to help children fighting cancer. After learning about Alex’s Lemonade Stand Foundation, she was inspired by the difference one young girl had made while facing serious challenges of her own. Ava therefore decided to start a lemonade stand in her neighbourhood and use the money raised to support childhood cancer research.What started as a small effort has continued for a decade now and Ava has raised $22,000 for Alex’s Lemonade Stand Foundation, an organisation that supports research into childhood cancer. According to This Is CNY, the money has helped fund 450 hours of cancer research.The initiative has also grown beyond a neighbourhood lemonade stand. Over the years, several local businesses and organisations have joined her efforts, helping turn the fundraiser into a community-supported activity.Ava's work has also earned her recognition among Central New York's outstanding high school students. She was among the 20 students honoured at the 2026 Best and Brightest Awards organised by Syracuse.com and The Post-Standard on November 5 at the Redhouse Arts Center in Syracuse.The awards recognise the achievements of high school seniors graduating in 2027. Students were selected based on their academic performance, extracurricular activities, leadership and contributions to their schools and communities.Ten years of helping cancer researchAva first came across Alex’s Lemonade Stand Foundation when she was eight. Learning about the work of the foundation inspired her to take action. She started a lemonade stand in her neighbourhood and began collecting money for paediatric cancer research.The initiative continued over the following years. What started with Ava selling lemonade gradually attracted support from different parts of the community.Wegmans, Costco, Walmart and the Onondaga County Sheriff's Office were among the organisations that contributed supplies and support. Their involvement helped Ava continue the fundraiser and expand its reach.Over 10 years, her efforts resulted in $22,000 being raised for the foundation. The amount has funded 450 hours of cancer research.Sarah McIntosh of Alex’s Lemonade Stand Foundation praised Ava's efforts and her ability to bring people together.“What Ava built with her lemonade stand shows her strong leadership skills and ability to rally people together to make a difference and to push for a better future,” McIntosh said.Ava's career plans shaped by fundraisingThe work also influenced how Ava looks at her future. Through her community service, she realised that an individual's efforts can make a difference.She is now pursuing her interest in criminal justice and forensics. Ava was selected for the BOCES New Visions Criminal Justice Program, where she continues to excel.After completing high school, she hopes to attend the University at Albany. She plans to study criminal justice and forensics, or digital forensics.Alongside her community work and academic interests, Ava is involved in several activities at school. She plays soccer and is a member of the girls' wrestling team. She is also part of the marching band and regularly volunteers at her church.Ava also manages several part-time jobs, including working as a youth soccer referee.Her selection for the Best and Brightest Awards recognises these achievements alongside her contribution to the community.The 2026 awards honoured 20 students from Central New York. Eligible students had to maintain at least a B grade or a 3.0 grade point average and attend schools in the region.Students submitted applications detailing their academic achievements, extracurricular activities and community service. articles.title: Gunman who killed 6 in Poland's Krakow square dies in hospital after police shootout
articles.summary: The Krakow shooter, 24, died Monday after police shot him during Saturday's mass shooting that killed six and wounded 15 in the historic square.
articles.body: The gunman who killed six people and wounded 15 others in a shooting at a crowded square in Poland died Monday after being shot by police during the attack, authorities said. The 24-year-old suspect had been hospitalized in critical condition since Saturday's shooting in Krakow and underwent several operations before his death. Polish prosecutors have opened an investigation into the killings and attempted killings, including attacks on police officers, as a possible terrorist offense. Authorities said the gunman held far-right views, though investigators have not publicly established a motive for the attack. The three are believed to have died from gunshot wounds, though authorities have not confirmed the circumstances of their deaths. The suspect, who was wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, drove into Krakow's historic Main Square on Saturday before opening fire, according to authorities. Four women and two men were killed, including a British man and an Austrian woman. Five foreign nationals were among the wounded. articles.title: Tamil Nadu man alleges TVK MLA assaulted him over civic grievances, later denies claim in video
articles.summary: PERAMBALUR: A controversy has erupted in Tamil Nadu after a man alleged that a TVK MLA assaulted him when he approached the legislator with complaints
articles.body: PERAMBALUR: A controversy has erupted in Tamil Nadu after a man alleged that a TVK MLA assaulted him when he approached the legislator with complaints about civic issues, including a drinking water shortage and garbage accumulation in his locality. However, the complainant later denied the assault allegations in a video recorded alongside the MLA.According to the complainant, Karthik Kumar, a resident of Kannan Biran Colony in Thuraiyur, his locality had been facing a drinking water shortage for the past week, while garbage had piled up in the area. He alleged that despite approaching municipal authorities, no action was taken to resolve the issues.Kumar also claimed that he had repeatedly attempted to contact his constituency MLA, Ravi Shankar, over the phone but received no response.On Diwali, Kumar, who had visited Mannachanallur for personal work, reportedly approached Ravi Shankar, who resides in the area, to raise the civic issues.Kumar alleged that the MLA verbally abused and physically assaulted him, including kicking him, before chasing him away. A video purportedly showing the incident went viral on social media, triggering criticism and raising questions about the conduct of an elected representative towards a constituent seeking redressal of civic grievances.The incident sparked a debate on social media, with users questioning the alleged behaviour of the legislator towards a constituent who had approached him over basic civic amenities.According to reports, Kumar is currently undergoing inpatient treatment at the Mannachanallur Government Hospital.Meanwhile, allegations have also emerged that police personnel asked Kumar to leave the hospital and warned him against filing a complaint against the MLA. These claims have not been independently verified.However, in a subsequent video recorded alongside Ravi Shankar, Kumar denied that the legislator had assaulted him and claimed that the incident was being misrepresented on social media.The contradictory claims have added another dimension to the controversy, with the incident drawing considerable attention across social media platforms.(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: 'Merely political posturing': Bangladesh says Hasina has no intention of returning from India
articles.summary: Bangladesh government on Monday said former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has no intention of returning to the country from India, amid reports that she
articles.body: Bangladesh government on Monday said former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has no intention of returning to the country from India, amid reports that she had sought a new passport and national identity card.Chief prosecutor Md Aminul Islam said Hasina's recent activities, as reported by various media outlets, were "merely political posturing"."Her recent activities, as reported by various media outlets, are merely political posturing," The Daily Star quoted Islam as saying."She is not taking the legal steps she should take to return to Bangladesh," he told journalists at his office.Asked about reports that Hasina had applied for a new passport, Islam reiterated, "For now, our comment is that she will not return and that these activities are political posturing."His remarks come days after Hasina expressed her intention to return to Bangladesh in December, despite facing serious legal challenges, including a death sentence handed down in absentia by a special tribunal over the deadly crackdown on protesters in 2024.Hasina has been living in India since fleeing Bangladesh in August 2024, following a student-led uprising that toppled her Awami League government.Meanwhile, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, Humayun Kobir, on Thursday ruled out issuing any travel document or passport to Hasina, describing her as a "fugitive terrorist" and a "dictator".Bangladesh has also sought Hasina's extradition from India, where she took refuge after leaving office.India has acknowledged receiving Bangladesh's extradition requests but is yet to announce a decision on handing her over.
